record.program_name: Richmond HUD funds (CDBG, HOME, Housing Choice Vouchers) administered by Contra Costa County: pointer record

City contact: City of Richmond Community Development Department, Housing Division (Jesus Morales, Housing Manager, 510-620-6649).
record.typical_award_size: Pointer record, not a separate pool. Richmond does not run its own CDBG or HOME program. The adopted Housing Element states that although Richmond is eligible to be a HUD entitlement city, after staffing cuts the City opted for Contra Costa County to receive its share of HUD funding, and that the County administers CDBG and HOME for Richmond; the County CDBG page defines the Urban County as the entire county less Antioch, Concord, Pittsburg and Walnut Creek, so Richmond is inside the Urban County and the County HOME Consortium. record.program_name: Inclusionary Housing Ordinance In-Lieu Fee Fund (Chapter 822-4)
record.administering_agency: Contra Costa County Department of Conservation and Development
record.typical_award_size: FY 2026/27: $1,216,295 available; awards $1,000,000 to Orbisonia Village (Pacific West, Bay Point, 167 units) and $216,295 to Harbor Pointe (USA Properties, Discovery Bay, 168 units). FY 2025/26: $1,054,134 awarded. Fees come from unincorporated projects of five or more units that pay in lieu of building 15% affordable units; the fee is set annually by the Board (for rentals, the 55-year gap between average two-bedroom rent and the affordable rent; for sale units, the gap between the affordable price and the countywide median sale price).
record.per_unit_cap: Mixed-income projects are capped at an award based on the number of 80% AMI or 50% AMI units that exceed the inclusionary requirement.
record.affordability_requirement: New construction for households up to 80% AMI, unincorporated county only; preference for two-bedroom and larger units and for projects exceeding the inclusionary minimum. Cannot fund units required by density bonus or inclusionary obligations. Forgivable low-interest loan reconveyed after five years in service as affordable housing.
record.next_deadline: December 7, 2026 at 5:00 PM through the County housing NOFA when a balance exists. The State and Local Funds page says in-lieu fees are allocated through the annual Affordable Housing NOFA, but the FY 2027/28 NOFA PDF names only CDBG-Housing, HOME and Measure X, so confirm an in-lieu balance with DCD. FY 2026/27 awards required commitments by July 1, 2026 (Orbisonia) and December 31, 2027 (Harbor Pointe).

Small and lumpy, about $1,000,000 to $1,200,000 a year, and limited to unincorporated areas (Bay Point, Discovery Bay, North Richmond, Rodeo, El Sobrante, Alamo). Standard terms: 3% simple interest, 55-year term, annual payments from residual receipts shared 75% to soft lenders pro rata and 25% to the borrower, special payment from 75% of cost savings, due on sale or refinance; the County will not cut its rate below the home city's rate. Davis-Bacon applies to HOME projects with 12 or more HOME-assisted units and CDBG projects with eight or more units; the developer must determine state prevailing wage, which turns on the County loan and the Labor Code 1720(c) exemptions. Build America Buy America applies to CDBG and HOME projects over $250,000. The County is the HUD entitlement for the Urban County (all of the county except Antioch, Concord, Pittsburg and Walnut Creek, which have their own CDBG) and lead of the Contra Costa HOME Consortium, so HOME can be used countywide including inside those four cities. Awards are sized by the HOME per-unit subsidy table and used as gap money for 4% and 9% tax credit deals; the FY 2026/27 Trinity Plaza and Lakeside awards are both acquisition-rehab recapitalizations. HOME-ARP ($12,108,330 allocation) is closed to new applications. The County staff report notes awards are made contingent on other commitments by Dec 31 of the following year, with recapture if unmet.

record.program_name: Innovative Housing Trust Fund (IHTF), County of San Diego
record.administering_agency: County of San Diego HHSA, Housing and Community Development Services (HCDS); established by the Board of Supervisors October 10, 2017 (Administrative Code Article XV, Sections 230.8 and 232.5)
record.typical_award_size: Board allocations total over $129 million through seven allocations since 2017 (General Fund one-time money, plus redirected grant balances such as $2 million of Capital ESG in June 2025). $112 million has been awarded to 36 developments with 3,054 units in 22 communities, leveraging $1.6 billion. record.typical_award_size: HHAP-6 allocations: County of San Joaquin $5,399,638.58 and San Joaquin Continuum of Care $5,766,906.84 (City of Stockton runs its own separate process; the regional HHAP-6 plan totals $22,698,332.21). Regional plan context: permanent housing about 18% of the regional budget, capital $0. HHAP-5 local awards: 30 agreements totaling $6,430,416.36 approved March 3, 2026, plus $1,000,000 HHAP-5 to the SJ BeWell Tiny Home Village.
record.per_unit_cap: Not applicable; no capital line in HHAP-6.
record.affordability_requirement: Housing First compliant projects serving people experiencing homelessness; HHAP-6 priorities are sustaining existing permanent and interim housing investments. Applicants must be 501(c)(3) nonprofits, tribes or public agencies.

record.layering_notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). HHAP has been used as a small capital and operating piece in County-area PSH (for example $1,000,000 in Lodi Commons and $1,000,000 HHAP-5 for the BeWell tiny home village), but the HHAP-6 regional plan budgets $0 for capital and shifts money to sustaining operations, so developers should treat HHAP as an operating or services source for existing PSH rather than a construction source. The 2025 Regional Homeless Action Plan reports 240 PSH units built in the past five years and 200 plus in the pipeline, and a shelter inventory growing from 1,346 to 1,934 beds by the end of 2026. HHAP rounds 1 through 6 brought roughly $82.7 million to the region. HUD CoC Program funds flow through the SJCoC annual competition (2024 announcement posted on sjchsa.org); Stockton, the County and the CoC file a joint HHAP action plan.

record.program_name: Density Bonus and Other Incentives, Manteca Municipal Code Chapter 17.72 (Ord. 1501, 2011) and Draft Zoning Code Update (public review October 22 to November 21, 2026)
record.administering_agency: City of Manteca Development Services Department, Planning Division
record.typical_award_size: Requirement and entitlement incentive, not a subsidy. One density bonus with concessions per Government Code 65915 for 10% lower income, 5% very low income, senior or 10% moderate for-sale units; parking caps of 1 space (0-1 bedroom), 2 (2-3 bedrooms), 2.5 (4 or more bedrooms); waivers of standards that physically preclude the project; density bonus agreement required; pro forma review consultant paid by applicant unless nonprofit. The Draft Zoning Code Update (implementing the 2043 General Plan and 6th Cycle Housing Element) rewrites 17.72 and the 17.200 density bonus definitions and makes Council the approval authority.
record.affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds; continued affordability per Government Code 65915 (55 years rental) under the agreement required by 17.72.030.
record.next_deadline: No application deadline; applies at entitlement. The Draft Zoning Code Update public review period runs October 22 through November 21, 2026 per the City Title 17 page (the draft's cover lists November 22, 2026); comments to planning@manteca.gov. The Planning Commission public hearing notice and General Plan Update EIR Addendum are listed on the City page but not yet posted, and no adoption date is stated.
record.layering_notes: Manteca's 2011 chapter has not kept pace with state law (no 50% or 100% bonus tiers, old parking ratios), so state law controls in practice; the pending Zoning Code Update should fix this. Section 17.72.030.G still references a Chapter 17.32 Affordable Housing Requirements that no longer exists in the code (see next record). Manteca has no local trust fund, in-lieu fund or NOFA, so the land-use incentive plus County and regional sources (Urban County CDBG and HOME, SJRHF, HACSJ PBVs, BHSA) are the whole local layer. Read from the zoneomics mirror of Title 17 (ecode360 blocks scripts); the City's Title 17 page confirms the update schedule.
record.prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

record.program_name: Below Market Rate (BMR) Housing Fund NOFA 2026/27
record.administering_agency: City of Menlo Park Community Development Department, Housing Division
record.typical_award_size: Approximately $4 million available for the production and preservation of permanent affordable housing, awarded competitively by the City Council; PlanetBids listing cites award sizes of about $300,000 to $800,000. Additional consideration for extremely low income units, special populations and preservation or rehabilitation of multifamily housing. Emergency shelters and transitional housing are not eligible. The prior round (January 2023) offered $1.5 million to $2 million; the City also contributed $1 million to a teacher housing project in November 2024.
record.affordability_requirement: Permanent affordability consistent with the BMR Housing Program Guidelines (October 21, 2025) and the Housing Element; priority to extremely low income and special needs units.
record.next_deadline: Applications due 5:00 pm Friday, November 20, 2026 on PlanetBids (invitation 2026-100926-101526; questions closed November 6, 2026); Housing Commission review winter 2027, Council award spring 2027. Housing Element Program H1.I requires a NOFA at least every two years.
record.layering_notes: County layer: every San Mateo County city project competes for the County Affordable Housing Fund NOFA (AHF 14 closed July 15, 2026, next fall 2027), HEART bridge loans and HACSM project-based vouchers; city money is usually the first commitment that unlocks those. The BMR fund is capitalized by commercial in-lieu fees (office and R&D $23.26 per square foot in FY 2026-27) and residential in-lieu payments, so its size tracks Meta and life science approvals; $4 million is enough for one gap loan or a preservation deal and is typically paired with County AHF and HACSM PBVs. Source is the City's 2026 NOFA page; contact Arianna Milton, ANMilton@menlopark.gov, (650) 330-6705.
record.prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. Local loans can be public funds under 1720(b)(1), (b)(4) or (b)(5), but 1720(c)(5)(E) exempts privately owned residential projects whose only public participation is below-market loans with at least 40% of units restricted for 20 or more years at 80% AMI or below, and 1720(c)(3) exempts de minimis subsidy. The Menlo Park NOFA page and 2026 draft NOFA announcement contain no prevailing wage term. https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720
